entries.e078204314a641b818d471f4d1c6acdee51bd197: <div sID="gen19573" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="10" osisID="Dan.10" sID="Dan.10"/> <div eID="gen19573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19574" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19575" type="x-p"/> This chapter and the two next (which conclude this book) make up one entire vision and prophecy, which was communicated to Daniel for the use of the church, not by signs and figures, as before (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.1-Dan.8.27">ch. vii. and viii.</reference>), but by express words; and this was about two years after the vision in the foregoing chapter. Daniel prayed daily, but had a vision only now and then. In this chapter we have some things introductory to the prophecy, in the eleventh chapter the particular predictions, and <reference osisRef="Dan.12.1-Dan.12.13">ch. xii.</reference> the conclusion of it. This chapter shows us, I. Daniel's solemn fasting and humiliation, before he had this vision, <reference osisRef="Dan.10.1-Dan.10.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. A glorious appearance of the Son of God to him, and the deep impression it made upon him, <reference osisRef="Dan.10.4-Dan.10.9">ver. 4-9</reference>. III. The encouragement that was given him to expect such a discovery of future events as should be satisfactory and useful both to others and to himself, and that he should be enabled both to understand the meaning of this discovery, though difficult, and to bear up under the lustre of it, though dazzling and dreadful, <reference osisRef="Dan.10.10-Dan.10.21">ver. 10-21</reference>.
entries.780dc083d8bb7b9de57f4ac485670830df378334: <div eID="gen19575" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19574" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Vision near the River Hiddekel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 534.)</title> <div sID="gen19576" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia a thing was revealed unto Daniel, whose name was called Belteshazzar; and the thing <hi type="italic">was</hi> true, but the time appointed <hi type="italic">was</hi> long: and he understood the thing, and had understanding of the vision. <hi type="super">2</hi> In those days I Daniel was mourning three full weeks. <hi type="super">3</hi> I ate no pleasant bread, neither came flesh nor wine in my mouth, neither did I anoint myself at all, till three whole weeks were fulfilled. <hi type="super">4</hi> And in the four and twentieth day of the first month, as I was by the side of the great river, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> Hiddekel; <hi type="super">5</hi> Then I lifted up mine eyes, and looked, and behold a certain man clothed in linen, whose loins <hi type="italic">were</hi> girded with fine gold of Uphaz: <hi type="super">6</hi> His body also <hi type="italic">was</hi> like the beryl, and his face as the appearance of lightning, and his eyes as lamps of fire, and his arms and his feet like in colour to polished brass, and the voice of his words like the voice of a multitude. <hi type="super">7</hi> And I Daniel alone saw the vision: for the men that were with me saw not the vision; but a great quaking fell upon them, so that they fled to hide themselves. <hi type="super">8</hi> Therefore I was left alone, and saw this great vision, and there remained no strength in me: for my comeliness was turned in me into corruption, and I retained no strength. <hi type="super">9</hi> Yet heard I the voice of his words: and when I heard the voice of his words, then was I in a deep sleep on my face, and my face toward the ground. <div eID="gen19576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19577" type="x-p"/> This vision is dated in the <hi type="italic">third year of Cyrus,</hi> that is, of his reign after the conquest of Babylon, his third year since Daniel became acquainted with him and a subject to him. Here is, <div eID="gen19577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19578" type="x-p"/> I. A general idea of this prophecy (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">The thing was true;</hi> every word of God is so; it was true that Daniel had such a vision, and that such and such things were said. This he solemnly attests upon the word of a prophet. <hi type="italic">Et hoc paratus est verificare—He was prepared to verify it;</hi> and, if it was a word <hi type="italic">spoken from heaven,</hi> no doubt it is stedfast and may be depended upon. <hi type="italic">But the time appointed was long,</hi> as long as to the end of the reign of Antiochus, which was 300 years, a long time indeed when it is looked upon as to come. Nay, and because it is usual with the prophets to glance at things spiritual and eternal, there is that in this prophecy which looks in type as far forward as to the end of the world and the resurrection of the dead; and then he might well say, <hi type="italic">The time appointed was long.</hi> It was, however, made as plain to him as if it had been a history rather than a prophecy; he <hi type="italic">understood the thing;</hi> so distinctly was it delivered to him, and received by him, that he could say he <hi type="italic">had understanding of the vision.</hi> It did not so much operate upon his fancy as upon his understanding. <div eID="gen19578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19579" type="x-p"/> II. An account of Daniel's mortification of himself before he had this vision, not in expectation of it, nor, when he prayed that solemn prayer <reference osisRef="Dan.9.1-Dan.9.27">ch. ix.</reference>, does it appear that he had any expectation of the vision in answer to it, but purely from a principle of devotion and pious sympathy with the afflicted people of God. He <hi type="italic">was mourning full three weeks</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.2">v. 2</reference>), for his own sins and the sins of his people, and their sorrows. Some think that the particular occasion of his mourning was slothfulness and indifference of many of the Jews, who, though they had liberty to return to their own land, continued still in the land of their captivity, not knowing how to value the privileges offered them; and perhaps it troubled him the more because those that did so justified themselves by the example of Daniel, though they had not that reason to stay behind which he had. Others think that it was because he heard of the obstruction given to the building of the temple by the enemies of the Jews, who <hi type="italic">hired counsellors against them, to frustrate their purpose</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.4.4-Ezra.4.5">Ezra iv. 4, 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">all the days of Cyrus,</hi> and gained their point from his son Cambyses, or Artaxerxes, who governed while Cyrus was absent in the Scythian war. Note, Good men cannot but mourn to see how slowly the work of God goes on in the world and what opposition it meets with, how weak its friends are and how active its enemies. During the days of Daniel's mourning he <hi type="italic">ate no pleasant bread;</hi> he could not live without meat, but he ate little, and very sparingly, and mortified himself in the quality as well as the quantity of what he ate, which may truly be reckoned fasting, and a token of humiliation and sorrow. He did not eat the pleasant bread he used to eat, but that which was course and unpalatable, which he would not be tempted to eat any more of than was just necessary to support nature. As ornaments, so delicacies, are very disagreeable to a day of humiliation. <hi type="italic">Daniel ate no flesh, drank no wine, nor anointed himself,</hi> for those three week's time, <reference osisRef="Dan.10.3">v. 3</reference>. Though he was now a very old man, and might plead that the decay of his nature required what was nourishing, though he was a very great man, and might plead that, being used to dainty meats, he could not do without them, it would prejudice his health if he were, yet, when it was both to testify and to assist his devotion, he could thus deny himself; let this be noted to the shame of many young people in the common ranks of life who cannot persuade themselves thus to deny themselves. <div eID="gen19579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19580" type="x-p"/> III. A description of that glorious person whom Daniel saw in vision, which, it is generally agreed, could be no other that Christ himself, the eternal Word. He was by the side of the river Hiddekel (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.4">v. 4</reference>), probably walking there, not for diversion, but devotion and contemplation, as Isaac walked in the field, to meditate; and, being a person of distinction, he had his servants attending him at some distance. There he <hi type="italic">looked up,</hi> and saw <hi type="italic">one man Christ Jesus.</hi> It must be he, for he appears in the same resemblance wherein he appeared to St. John in the isle of Patmos, <reference osisRef="Rev.1.13-Rev.1.15">Rev. i. 13-15</reference>. His dress was priestly, for he is the high priest of our profession, <hi type="italic">clothed in linen,</hi> as the high priest himself was on the day of atonement, that great day; <hi type="italic">his loins were girded</hi> (in St. John's vision his <hi type="italic">paps</hi> were <hi type="italic">girded) with a golden girdle</hi> of the finest gold, that of Uphaz, for every thing about Christ is the best in its kind. The <hi type="italic">girding of the loins</hi> denotes his ready and diligent application to his work, as his Father's servant, in the business of our redemption. His shape was amiable, <hi type="italic">his body like the beryl,</hi> a precious stone of a sky-colour. His countenance was awful, and enough to strike a terror on the beholders, for his face was <hi type="italic">as the appearance of lightning,</hi> which dazzles the eyes, both brightens and threatens. His <hi type="italic">eyes</hi> were bright and sparkling, <hi type="italic">as lamps of fire.</hi> His <hi type="italic">arms and feet</hi> shone <hi type="italic">like polished brass,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.10.6">v. 6</reference>. His <hi type="italic">voice</hi> was loud, and strong, and very piercing, <hi type="italic">like the voice of a multitude.</hi> The <hi type="italic">vox Dei</hi>—<hi type="italic">voice of God</hi> can overpower the <hi type="italic">vox populi</hi>—<hi type="italic">voice of the people.</hi> Thus glorious did Christ appear, and it should engage us, 1. To think highly and honourably of him. <hi type="italic">Now consider how great this man is,</hi> and in all things let him have the pre-eminence. 2. To admire his condescension for us and our salvation. Over all this splendour he drew a veil when he took upon him the form of a servant, and <hi type="italic">emptied himself.</hi> <div eID="gen19580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19581" type="x-p"/> IV. The wonderful influence that this appearance had upon Daniel and his attendants, and the terror that it struck upon him and them. <div eID="gen19581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19582" type="x-p"/> 1. His attendants <hi type="italic">saw not the vision;</hi> it was not fit that they should be honoured with the sight of it. There is a divine revelation vouchsafed to all, from converse with which none are excluded who do not exclude themselves; but such a vision must be peculiar to Daniel, who was a favourite. Paul's companions were aware of the <hi type="italic">light,</hi> but <hi type="italic">saw no man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.9.7">Acts ix. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.22.9">xxii. 9</reference>. Note, It is the honour of those who are beloved of God that, what is hidden from others, is known to them. Christ <hi type="italic">manifests himself to them, but not to the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.14.22">John xiv. 22</reference>. But, though they saw not the vision, they were seized with an unaccountable trembling; either from the voice they heard, or from some strange concussion or vibration of the air they felt, so it was that a <hi type="italic">great quaking fell upon them, so that they fled to hide themselves,</hi> probably among the willows that grew by the river's side. Note, Many have a <hi type="italic">spirit of bondage to fear</hi> who never receive <hi type="italic">a spirit of adoption,</hi> to whom Christ has been, and will be, never otherwise than a terror. Now the fright that Daniel's attendants were in is a confirmation of the truth of the vision; it could not be Daniel's fancy, or the product of a heated imagination of his own, for it had a real, powerful, and strange effect upon those about him. <div eID="gen19582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19583" type="x-p"/> 2. He himself saw it, and saw it alone, but he was not able to bear the sight of it. It not only dazzled his eyes, but overwhelmed his spirit, so that <hi type="italic">there remained no strength in him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.10.8">v. 8</reference>. He said, as Moses himself, <hi type="italic">I exceedingly fear and quake.</hi> His spirits were all so employed, either in an intense speculation of the glory of this vision or in the fortifying of his heart against the terror of it, that his body was left in a manner lifeless and spiritless. He had no vigour in him, and was but one remove from a dead carcase; he looked as pale as death, his colour was gone, his <hi type="italic">comeliness</hi> in him was <hi type="italic">turned into corruption,</hi> and he <hi type="italic">retained no strength.</hi> Note, the greatest and best of men cannot bear the immediate discoveries of the divine glory; no man can see it and live; it is next to death to see a glimpse of it, as Daniel here; but glorified saints see Christ as he is and can bear the sight. But, though Daniel was thus dispirited with the vision of Christ, yet he <hi type="italic">heard the voice of his words</hi> and knew what he said. Note, We must take heed lest our reverence of God's glory, by which we should be awakened to hear his voice both in his word and in his providence, should degenerate into such a dread of him as will disable or indispose us to hear it. It should seem that when the vision of Christ terrified Daniel the voice of his words soon pacified and composed him, silenced his fear, and laid him to sleep in a holy security and serenity of mind: <hi type="italic">When I heard the voice of his words I fell into a slumber,</hi> a sweet slumber, <hi type="italic">on my face,</hi> and <hi type="italic">my face towards the ground.</hi> When he saw the vision he threw himself prostrate, into a posture of the most humble adoration, and dropped asleep, not as careless of what he heard and saw, but charmed with it. Note, How dreadful soever Christ may appear to those who are under convictions of sin, and in terror by reason of it, there is enough in his word to quiet their spirits and make them easy, if they will but attend to it and apply it.
entries.39c930511cb2646f1c616d61e05853dbe03fd76c: <div eID="gen19583" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Daniel Alarmed and Comforted. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 534.)</title> <div sID="gen19584" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> And, behold, a hand touched me, which set me upon my knees and <hi type="italic">upon</hi> the palms of my hands. <hi type="super">11</hi> And he said unto me, O Daniel, a man greatly beloved, understand the words that I speak unto thee, and stand upright: for unto thee am I now sent. And when he had spoken this word unto me, I stood trembling. <hi type="super">12</hi> Then said he unto me, Fear not, Daniel: for from the first day that thou didst set thine heart to understand, and to chasten thyself before thy God, thy words were heard, and I am come for thy words. <hi type="super">13</hi> But the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me one and twenty days: but, lo, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me; and I remained there with the kings of Persia. <hi type="super">14</hi> Now I am come to make thee understand what shall befall thy people in the latter days: for yet the vision <hi type="italic">is</hi> for <hi type="italic">many</hi> days. <hi type="super">15</hi> And when he had spoken such words unto me, I set my face toward the ground, and I became dumb. <hi type="super">16</hi> And, behold, <hi type="italic">one</hi> like the similitude of the sons of men touched my lips: then I opened my mouth, and spake, and said unto him that stood before me, O my lord, by the vision my sorrows are turned upon me, and I have retained no strength. <hi type="super">17</hi> For how can the servant of this my lord talk with this my lord? for as for me, straightway there remained no strength in me, neither is there breath left in me. <hi type="super">18</hi> Then there came again and touched me <hi type="italic">one</hi> like the appearance of a man, and he strengthened me, <hi type="super">19</hi> And said, O man greatly beloved, fear not: peace <hi type="italic">be</hi> unto thee, be strong, yea, be strong. And when he had spoken unto me, I was strengthened, and said, Let my lord speak; for thou hast strengthened me. <hi type="super">20</hi> Then said he, Knowest thou wherefore I come unto thee? and now will I return to fight with the prince of Persia: and when I am gone forth, lo, the prince of Grecia shall come. <hi type="super">21</hi> But I will show thee that which is noted in the scripture of truth: and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none that holdeth with me in these things, but Michael your prince. <div eID="gen19584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19585" type="x-p"/> Much ado here is to bring Daniel to be able to bear what Christ has to say to him. Still we have him in a fright, hardly and very slowly recovering himself; but he is still answered and <hi type="italic">supported</hi> with <hi type="italic">good words</hi> and <hi type="italic">comfortable words.</hi> Let us see how Daniel is by degrees brought to himself, and gather up the several passages that are to the same purport. <div eID="gen19585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19586" type="x-p"/> I. Daniel is in a great consternation and finds it very difficult to get clear of it. The hand that <hi type="italic">touched him</hi> set him at first <hi type="italic">upon his knees and the palms of his hands,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.10.10">v. 10</reference>. Note, Strength and comfort commonly come by degrees to those that have been long cast down and disquieted; they are first helped up a little, and then more. <hi type="italic">After two days he will revive us, and</hi> then <hi type="italic">the third day he will raise us up.</hi> And we must not <hi type="italic">despise the day of small things,</hi> but be thankful for the beginnings of mercy. Afterwards he is helped up, but he <hi type="italic">stands trembling</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.11">v. 11</reference>), for fear lest he fall again. Note, Before God <hi type="italic">gives strength and power unto his people</hi> he makes them sensible of their own weakness. <hi type="italic">I trembled in myself, that I might rest in the day of trouble,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.3.16">Hab. iii. 16</reference>. But when, afterwards, Daniel recovered so much strength in his limbs that he could stand steadily, yet he tells us (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.15">v. 15</reference>) that he <hi type="italic">set his face towards the ground and became dumb;</hi> he was as a man astonished, who knew not what to say, struck dumb with admiration and fear, and was loth to enter into discourse with one so far <hi type="italic">above him;</hi> he <hi type="italic">kept silence,</hi> yea, <hi type="italic">even from good,</hi> till he had recollected himself a little. Well, at length he recovered, not only the use of his feet, but the use of his tongue; and, when he <hi type="italic">opened his mouth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.16">v. 16</reference>), that which he had to say was to excuse his having been so long silent, for really he durst not speak, he could not speak: "<hi type="italic">O my lord</hi>" (so, in great humility, this prophet calls the angel, though the angels, in great humility, called themselves <hi type="italic">fellow-servants to the prophets,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.22.9">Rev. xxii. 9</reference>), "<hi type="italic">by the vision my sorrows are turned upon me;</hi> they break in up on me with violence; the sense of my sinful sorrowful state <hi type="italic">turns upon me</hi> when I see thy purity and brightness." Note, Man, who has lost his integrity, has reason to blush, and be ashamed of himself, when he sees or considers the glory of the blessed angels that keep their integrity. "<hi type="italic">My sorrows are turned upon me, and I have retained no strength</hi> to resist them or bear up a head against them." And again (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.17">v. 17</reference>), like one half dead with the fright, he complains, "As for me, <hi type="italic">straightway there remained no strength in me</hi> to receive these displays of the divine glory and these discoveries of the divine will; nay, <hi type="italic">there is no breath left in me.</hi>" Such a <hi type="italic">deliquium</hi> did he suffer that he could not draw one breath after another, but panted and languished, and was in a manner breathless. See how well it is for us that the treasure of divine revelation is put into <hi type="italic">earthen vessels,</hi> that God speaks to us <hi type="italic">by men like ourselves</hi> and not by angels. Whatever we may wish, in a peevish dislike of the method God takes in dealing with us, it is certain that if we were tried we should all be of Israel's mind at Mt. Sinai, when they said to Moses, <hi type="italic">Speak thou to us, and we will hear, but let not God speak to us lest we die,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.20.19">Exod. xx. 19</reference>. If Daniel could not bear it, how could we? Now this he insists upon as an excuse for his irreverent silence, which otherwise would have been blame-worthy: <hi type="italic">How can the servant of this my lord talk with this my lord?</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.10.17">v. 17</reference>. Note, Whenever we enter into communion with God it becomes us to have a due sense of the vast distance and disproportion that there are between us and the holy angels, and of the infinite distance, and no proportion at all, between us and the holy God, and to acknowledge that we cannot <hi type="italic">order our speech by reason of darkness.</hi> How shall we that are dust and ashes speak to the Lord of glory? <div eID="gen19586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19587" type="x-p"/> II. The blessed angel that was employed by Christ to converse with him gave him all the encouragement and comfort that could be. It should seem, it was not he whose glory he saw in vision (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.5-Dan.10.6">v. 5, 6</reference>) that here <hi type="italic">touched him,</hi> and <hi type="italic">talked with him;</hi> that was Christ, but this seems to have been the angel Gabriel, whom Christ had once before ordered to instruct Daniel, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.16">ch. viii. 16</reference>. That glorious appearance (as that of the <hi type="italic">God of glory</hi> to Abraham, <reference osisRef="Acts.7.2">Acts vii. 2</reference>) was to give authority and to gain attention to what the angel should say. Christ himself comforted John when he in a like case <hi type="italic">fell at his feet as dead</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.17">Rev. i. 17</reference>); but here he did it by <hi type="italic">the angel,</hi> whom Daniel saw in a glory much inferior to that of the vision in the verses before; for he was <hi type="italic">like the similitude of the sons of men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.16">v. 16</reference>), one like the appearance <hi type="italic">of a man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.10.18">v. 18</reference>. When <hi type="italic">he</hi> only <hi type="italic">appeared,</hi> as he had done before (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.21">ch. ix. 21</reference>), we do not find that Daniel was put into any disorder by it, as he was by this vision; and therefore he is here employed a third time with Daniel. <div eID="gen19587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19588" type="x-p"/> 1. He lent him his hand to help him, <hi type="italic">touched him, and set him upon his hands and knees</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.10">v. 10</reference>), else he would still have lain grovelling, <hi type="italic">touched his lips</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.16">v. 16</reference>), else he would have been still dumb; again he <hi type="italic">touched him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.18">v. 18</reference>), and put strength into him, else he would still have been staggering and trembling. Note, The hand of God's power going along with the word of his grace is alone effectual to redress all our grievances, and to rectify whatever is amiss in us. One touch from heaven brings us to our knees, sets us on our feet, opens our lips, and strengthens us; for it is God that works on us, and <hi type="italic">works in us, both to will and to do</hi> that which is good. <div eID="gen19588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19589" type="x-p"/> 2. He assured him of the great favour that God had for him: Thou art <hi type="italic">a man greatly beloved</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.11">v. 11</reference>); and again (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.19">v. 19</reference>), <hi type="italic">O man greatly beloved!</hi> Note, Nothing is more likely, nothing more effectual, to revive the drooping spirits of the saints than to be assured of God's love to them. Those are greatly beloved indeed whom God loves; and it is comfort enough to know it. <div eID="gen19589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19590" type="x-p"/> 3. He silenced his fears, and encouraged his hopes, with good words and comfortable words. He said unto him, <hi type="italic">Fear not, Daniel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.12">v. 12</reference>); and again (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.19">v. 19</reference>), <hi type="italic">O man greatly beloved! fear not; peace be unto thee; be strong, yea, be strong.</hi> Never did any tender mother quiet her child, when any thing had grieved or frightened it, with more compassion and affection than the angel here quieted Daniel. Those that are beloved of God have no reason to be afraid of any evil; peace is to them; God himself speaks peace to them; and they ought, upon the warrant of that, to speak peace to themselves; and that peace, that <hi type="italic">joy of the Lord,</hi> will be <hi type="italic">their strength.</hi> Will God <hi type="italic">plead against us with his great power?</hi> will he take advantage against us of our being overcome by his terror? <hi type="italic">No, but he will put strength into us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.23.6">Job xxiii. 6</reference>. So he did into Daniel here, when, by reason of the lustre of the vision, <hi type="italic">no strength</hi> of his own <hi type="italic">remained in him;</hi> and he acknowledges it (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">When he had spoken to me I was strengthened.</hi> Note, God by his word puts life, and strength, and spirit into his people; for if he says, <hi type="italic">Be strong,</hi> power goes along with the word. And, now that Daniel has experienced the efficacy of God's strengthening word and grace, he is ready for any thing: "<hi type="italic">Now, Let my lord speak,</hi> and I can hear it, I can bear it, and am ready to do according to it, <hi type="italic">for thou hast strengthened me.</hi>" Note, To those that (like Daniel here) have no might God <hi type="italic">increases strength,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.40.29">Isa. xl. 29</reference>. And we cannot keep up our communion with God but by strength derived from him; but, when he is pleased to put strength into us, we must make a good use of it, and say, <hi type="italic">Speak, Lord, for thy servant hears.</hi> Let God enable us to comply with his will, and then, whatever it is, we will stand complete in it. <hi type="italic">Da quod jubes, et jube quod vis—Give what thou commandest, and then command what thou wilt.</hi> <div eID="gen19590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19591" type="x-p"/> 4. He assured him that his fastings and prayers had come up for a memorial before God, as the angel told Cornelius (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.4">Acts x. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Fear not, Daniel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.10.12">v. 12</reference>. It is natural to fallen man to be afraid of an extraordinary messenger from heaven, as dreading to hear evil tidings thence; but Daniel need not fear, for he has by his three weeks' humiliation and supplication sent <hi type="italic">extraordinary</hi> messengers to heaven, which he may expect to return with an olive-branch of peace: "<hi type="italic">From the first day that thou didst set thy heart to understand</hi> the word of God, which is to be the rule of thy prayers, and to <hi type="italic">chasten thyself before thy God,</hi> that thou mightest put an edge upon thy prayers, <hi type="italic">thy words were heard,</hi>" as, before, <hi type="italic">at the beginning of thy supplication,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.9.23">ch. ix. 23</reference>. Note, As the <hi type="italic">entrance of God's word is enlightening</hi> to the upright, so the entrance of their prayers is pleasing to God, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.130">Ps. cxix. 130</reference>. From the first day that we begin to look towards God in a way of duty he is ready to meet us in a way of mercy. Thus ready is God to hear prayer. <hi type="italic">I said, I will confess, and thou forgavest.</hi> <div eID="gen19591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19592" type="x-p"/> 5. He informed him that he was sent to him on purpose to bring him a prediction of the future state of the church, as a token of God's accepting his prayers for the church: "<hi type="italic">Knowest thou wherefore I come unto thee?</hi> If thou knewest on what errand I come, thou wouldst not be put into such a consternation by it." Note, If we rightly understood the meaning of God's dealings with us, and the methods of his providence and grace concerning us, we should be better reconciled to them. "<hi type="italic">I have come for thy words</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.12">v. 12</reference>), to bring thee a gracious answer to thy prayers." Thus, when God's praying people call to him, he says, <hi type="italic">Here I am</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.9">Isa. lviii. 9</reference>); <hi type="italic">what would you</hi> have with me? See the power of prayer, what glorious things it has, in its time, fetched from heaven, what strange discoveries! On what errand did this angel come to Daniel? He tells him (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have come to make thee understand what shall befal thy people in the latter days.</hi> Daniel was a curious inquisitive man, that had all his days been searching into secret things, and it would be a great gratification to him to be let into the knowledge of things to come. Daniel had always been concerned for the church; its interests lay much upon his heart, and it would be a particular satisfaction to him to know what its state should be, and he would know the better what to pray for as long as he lived. He was now lamenting the difficulties which his people met with in the present day; but, that he might not be offended in those, the angel must tell him what greater difficulties are yet before them; and, if they be <hi type="italic">wearied</hi> now that they only <hi type="italic">run with the footmen, how will they contend with horses?</hi> Note, It would abate our resentment of present troubles to consider that we know not but much greater are before us, which we are concerned to provide for. Daniel must be made to know what shall befal his people <hi type="italic">in the latter days</hi> of the church, after the cessation of prophecy, and when the time drew nigh for the Messiah to appear, <hi type="italic">for yet the vision is for many days;</hi> the principal things that this vision was intended to give the church the foresight of would come to pass in the days of Antiochus, nearly 300 years after this. Now that which the angel is entrusted to communicate to Daniel, and which Daniel is encouraged to expect from him, is not any curious speculations, moral prognostications, nor rational prospects of his own, though he is an angel, but what he has <hi type="italic">received from the Lord.</hi> It was the <hi type="italic">revelation of Jesus Christ</hi> that the angel gave to St. John to be <hi type="italic">delivered to the churches,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.1.1">Rev. i. 1</reference>. So here (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will show thee what is written in the scriptures of truth,</hi> that is, what is fixed in the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God. The <hi type="italic">decree of God</hi> is a thing written, it is a <hi type="italic">scripture</hi> which remains and cannot be altered. <hi type="italic">What I have written I have written.</hi> As there are scriptures for the revealed will of God, the letters-patent, which are published to the world, so there are scriptures for the secret will of God, the close rolls, which are <hi type="italic">sealed among his treasures,</hi> the book of his decrees. Both are <hi type="italic">scriptures of truth;</hi> nothing shall be added to nor taken from either of them. The <hi type="italic">secret things belong not to us,</hi> only now and then some few paragraphs have been copied out from the book of God's counsels, and delivered to the prophets for the use of the church, as here to Daniel; but they are the <hi type="italic">things revealed,</hi> even the <hi type="italic">words of this law,</hi> which belong <hi type="italic">to us and to our children;</hi> and we are concerned to study what is written in these <hi type="italic">scriptures of truth,</hi> for they are things which <hi type="italic">belong to our everlasting peace.</hi> <div eID="gen19592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19593" type="x-p"/> 6. He gave him a general account of the adversaries of the church's cause, from whom it might be expected that troubles would arise, and of its patrons, under whose protection it might be assured of safety and victory at last. (1.) The <hi type="italic">kings of the earth</hi> are and will be its adversaries; for they set themselves against the Lord, and against his Anointed, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.2">Ps. ii. 2</reference>. The angel told Daniel that he was to have come to him with a gracious answer to his prayers, but that the <hi type="italic">prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood him one and twenty days,</hi> just the three weeks that Daniel had been fasting and praying. Cambyses king of Persia had been very busy to embarrass the affairs of the Jews, and to do them all the mischief he could, and the angel had been all that time employed to counter-work him; so that he had been constrained to defer his visit to Daniel till now, for angels can be but in one place at a time. Or, as Dr. Lightfoot says, This new king of Persia, by hindering the temple, had hindered those good tidings which otherwise he should have brought him. The kings and kingdoms of the world were indeed sometimes helpful to the church, but more often they were injurious to it. "When <hi type="italic">I have gone forth</hi> from the kings of Persia, when their monarchy is brought down for their unkindness to the Jews, then <hi type="italic">the prince of Grecia shall come,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Dan.10.20">v. 20</reference>. The Grecian monarchy, though favourable to the Jews at first, as the Persian was, will yet come to be vexatious to them. Such is the state of the church-militant; when it has got clear of one enemy it has another to encounter: and such a hydra's head is that of the old serpent; when one storm has <hi type="italic">blown over</hi> it is not long before another rises. (2.) The <hi type="italic">God of heaven</hi> is, and will be, its protector, and, under him, the angels of heaven are its patrons and guardians. [1.] Here is the angel Gabriel busy in the service of the church, making his part good in defence of it twenty-one days, <hi type="italic">against the prince of Persia,</hi> and <hi type="italic">remaining there with the kings of Persia,</hi> as consul, or liege-ambassador, to take care of the affairs of the Jews in that court, and to do them service, <reference osisRef="Dan.10.13">v. 13</reference>. And, though much was done against them by the kings of Persia (God permitting it), it is probably that much more mischief would have been done them, and they would have been quite ruined (witness Haman's plot) if God had not prevented it by the ministration of angels. Gabriel resolves, when he has despatched this errand to Daniel, that he will return <hi type="italic">to fight with the prince of Persia,</hi> will continue to oppose him, and will at length humble and bring down that proud monarchy (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.20">v. 20</reference>), though he knows that another as mischievous, even that of Grecia, will rise instead of it. [2.] Here is Michael our prince, the great protector of the church, and the patron of its just but injured cause: <hi type="italic">The first of the chief princes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.10.13">v. 13</reference>. Some understand it not of a created angel, but an archangel of the highest order, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.16">1 Thess. iv. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jude.1.9">Jude 9</reference>. Others think that <hi type="italic">Michael the archangel</hi> is no other than Christ himself, the <hi type="italic">angel of the covenant,</hi> and the Lord of the angels, he whom Daniel saw in vision, <reference osisRef="Dan.10.5">v. 5</reference>. He <hi type="italic">came to help me</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.13">v. 13</reference>); and there is <hi type="italic">none but he that holds with me in these things,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.10.21">v. 21</reference>. Christ is the church's prince; angels are not, <reference osisRef="Heb.2.5">Heb. ii. 5</reference>. He presides in the affairs of the church and effectually provides for its good. He is said to <hi type="italic">hold with the angels,</hi> for it is he that makes them serviceable to the <hi type="italic">heirs of salvation;</hi> and, if he were not on the church's side, its case were bad. But, says David, and so says the church, <hi type="italic">The Lord takes my part with those that help me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.118.7">Ps. cxviii. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">The Lord is with those that uphold my soul,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.54.4">Ps. liv. 4</reference>.  <chapter eID="Dan.10"/> <div eID="gen19593" type="x-p"/>

entries.d2bac70ed337aa57c144c41c5e5a680312b6e873: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12163"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 10</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Dan.10.1-Dan.10.21">Da 10:1-21</reference>. Daniel Comforted by an Angelic Vision.</title> <div sID="gen22055" type="x-p"/> The tenth through twelfth chapters more fully describe the vision in the eighth chapter by a second vision on the same subject, just as the vision in the seventh chapter explains more fully that in the second. The tenth chapter is the prologue; the eleventh, the prophecy itself; and the twelfth, the epilogue. The tenth chapter unfolds the spiritual worlds as the background of the historical world (<reference osisRef="Job.1.7">Job 1:7</reference>; 2:1, &c.; <reference osisRef="Zech.3.1">Zec 3:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.2">2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.12.7">Re 12:7</reference>), and angels as the ministers of God's government of men. As in the world of nature (<reference osisRef="John.5.4">Joh 5:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.7.1-Rev.7.3">Re 7:1-3</reference>), so in that of history here; Michael, the champion of Israel, and with him another angel, whose aim is to realize God's will in the heathen world, resist the God-opposed spirit of the world. These struggles are not merely symbolical, but real (<reference osisRef="1Sam.16.13-1Sam.16.15">1Sa 16:13-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.22">1Ki 22:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.6.12">Ep 6:12</reference>).<div eID="gen22055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22056" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12163"/><hi type="bold">1. third year of Cyrus--</hi>two years after Cyrus' decree for the restoration of the Jews had gone forth, in accordance with Daniel's prayer in <reference osisRef="Dan.9.3-Dan.9.19">Da 9:3-19</reference>. This vision gives not merely general outlines, or symbols, but minute details of the future, in short, anticipative history. It is the expansion of the vision in <reference osisRef="Dan.8.1-Dan.8.14">Da 8:1-14</reference>. That which then "none understood," he says here, "he understood"; the messenger being sent to him for this (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.11">Da 10:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.10.14">14</reference>), to make him understand it. Probably Daniel was no longer in office at court; for in <reference osisRef="Dan.1.21">Da 1:21</reference>, it is said, "Daniel continued even unto the first year of King Cyrus"; not that he died then. See on <reference osisRef="Dan.1.21">Da 1:21</reference>.<div eID="gen22056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22057" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but the time appointed was long--</hi>rather, "it (that is, the prophecy) referred to great calamity" [Maurer]; or, "long and calamitous warfare" [Gesenius]. Literally, "host going to war"; hence, warfare, calamity. <div eID="gen22057" type="x-p"/>
entries.360d700ce44c3cc0fd2f6215b5ab9e848c5e937e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12164"/><div sID="gen22058" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12164"/><hi type="bold">2. mourning--</hi>that is, afflicting myself by fasting from "pleasant bread, flesh and wine" (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.3">Da 10:3</reference>), as a sign of sorrow, not for its own sake. Compare <reference osisRef="Matt.9.14">Mt 9:14</reference>, "fast," answering to "mourn" (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.15">Da 10:15</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.8">1Co 8:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.3">1Ti 4:3</reference>, which prove that "fasting" is not an indispensable Christian obligation; but merely an outward expression of sorrow, and separation from ordinary worldly enjoyments, in order to give one's self to prayer (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.2">Ac 13:2</reference>). Daniel's mourning was probably for his countrymen, who met with many obstructions to their building of the temple, from their adversaries in the Persian court. <div eID="gen22058" type="x-p"/>
entries.345427f68325306b24c04f40350756e83784ed33: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12165"/><div sID="gen22059" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12165"/><hi type="bold">3. no pleasant bread--</hi>"unleavened bread, even the bread of affliction" (<reference osisRef="Deut.16.3">De 16:3</reference>).<div eID="gen22059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22060" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">anoint--</hi>The Persians largely used unguents. <div eID="gen22060" type="x-p"/>
entries.70384dbf6af2983ae893d3d6bb407ce86708255e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12166"/><div sID="gen22061" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12166"/><hi type="bold">4. first month--</hi>Nisan, the month most suited for considering Israel's calamity, being that in which the feast of unleavened bread reminded them of their Egyptian bondage. Daniel mourned not merely for the seven days appointed (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.18">Ex 12:18</reference>), from the evening of the fourteenth to the twenty-first of Nisan, but thrice seven days, to mark extraordinary sorrow. His mourning ended on the twenty-first day, the closing day of the passover feast; but the vision is not till the twenty-fourth, because of the opposition of "the prince of Persia" (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.13">Da 10:13</reference>).<div eID="gen22061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22062" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I was by ... the ... river--</hi>in waking reality, not a trance (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.7">Da 10:7</reference>); when younger, he saw the future in images, but now when old, he receives revelations from angels in common language, that is, in the apocalyptic mode. In the patriarchal period God often appeared visibly, that is, theophany. In the prophets, next in the succession, the inward character of revelation is prominent. The consummation is when the seer looks up from earth into the unseen world, and has the future shown to him by angels, that is, apocalypse. So in the New Testament there is a parallel progression: God in the flesh, the spiritual activity of the apostles and the apocalypse [Auberlen].<div eID="gen22062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22063" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hiddekel--</hi>the Tigris. <div eID="gen22063" type="x-p"/>
entries.c151f9506e376187fb3a00d576e7d19857466e2d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12167"/><div sID="gen22064" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12167"/><hi type="bold">5. lifted up mine eyes--</hi>from the ground on which they had been fixed in his mourning.<div eID="gen22064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22065" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">certain man--</hi>literally, "one man." An angel of the highest order; for in <reference osisRef="Dan.8.16">Da 8:16</reference> he commands Gabriel to make Daniel to understand the vision, and in <reference osisRef="Dan.12.6">Da 12:6</reference> one of the two angels inquires of him how long it would be till the end predicted.<div eID="gen22065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22066" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">linen--</hi>the raiment of priests, being the symbol of sanctity, as more pure than wool (<reference osisRef="Exod.28.42">Ex 28:42</reference>); also of prophets (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.1">Jr 13:1</reference>); and of angels (<reference osisRef="Rev.15.6">Re 15:6</reference>).<div eID="gen22066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22067" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">girded with ... gold--</hi>that is, with a girdle interwoven with gold (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.13">Re 1:13</reference>). <div eID="gen22067" type="x-p"/>
entries.1a0c4989998a4586fcb61a6926ee73266aee578b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12168"/><div sID="gen22068" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12168"/><hi type="bold">6. beryl--</hi>literally, "Tarshish," in Spain. The beryl, identical with the chrysolite or topaz, was imported into the East from Tarshish, and therefore is called "the Tarshish stone." <div eID="gen22068" type="x-p"/>
entries.04ec9441d009e5d51b94e991d0bb37fe62999f91: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12169"/><div sID="gen22069" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12169"/><hi type="bold">7. they fled--</hi>terrified by the presence of the presence of the angel. <div eID="gen22069" type="x-p"/>
entries.bcc844d62ddeb93f94982ceba38a912cd3ec6f4c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12170"/><div sID="gen22070" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12170"/><hi type="bold">8. comeliness--</hi>literally, "vigor," that is, lively expression and color.<div eID="gen22070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22071" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">into corruption--</hi>"deadliness," that is, death-like paleness (<reference osisRef="Dan.5.6">Da 5:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.7.28">7:28</reference>). <div eID="gen22071" type="x-p"/>
entries.123b3e8dbf56a2da6cbe7008ffe51884c673dedb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12171"/><div sID="gen22072" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12171"/><hi type="bold">9. voice of his words--</hi>the sound of his words.<div eID="gen22072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22073" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was I in a deep sleep--</hi>"I sank into a deep sleep" [Lengkerke]. <div eID="gen22073" type="x-p"/>
entries.0600ed3e7be0069be77af5bb83a85a84f75e5d39: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12172"/><div sID="gen22074" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12172"/><hi type="bold">10. an hand--</hi>namely, of Gabriel, who interpreted other revelations to Daniel (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.16">Da 8:16</reference>) [Theodoret].<div eID="gen22074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22075" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set me upon my knees--</hi>Gesenius translates, "cause me to reel on my knees," &c. <div eID="gen22075" type="x-p"/>
entries.78345a0d4750e7b644ff1522c720c45bbf108087: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12173"/><div sID="gen22076" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12173"/><hi type="bold">11. man ... beloved--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Dan.9.23">Da 9:23</reference>).<div eID="gen22076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22077" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">understand--</hi>"attend to." See <reference osisRef="Dan.8.17">Da 8:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.18">18</reference>. <div eID="gen22077" type="x-p"/>
entries.dbaaeb4a34b60dd3d73f4c408a1d090c99897a69: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12174"/><div sID="gen22078" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12174"/><hi type="bold">12. Fear not--</hi>Be not affrighted at my presence.<div eID="gen22078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22079" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">didst set thine heart to understand--</hi>what shall come to pass to thy people at the last times (compare <reference osisRef="Dan.10.14">Da 10:14</reference>).<div eID="gen22079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22080" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chasten thyself--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Dan.10.2">Da 10:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.10.3">3</reference>).<div eID="gen22080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22081" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy words were heard--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Acts.10.4">Ac 10:4</reference>). Prayer is heard at once in heaven, though the sensible answer may seem to be delayed. God's messenger was detained on the way (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.13">Da 10:13</reference>) by the opposition of the powers of darkness. If in our prayers amidst long protracted sorrows we believed God's angel is on his way to us, what consolation it would give us!<div eID="gen22081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22082" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for thy words--</hi>because of thy prayers. <div eID="gen22082" type="x-p"/>
entries.6a786f878c16cb2086396e9569cf708401d2058b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12175"/><div sID="gen22083" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12175"/><hi type="bold">13. prince of ... Persia--</hi>the angel of darkness that represented the Persian world power, to which Israel was then subject. This verse gives the reason why, though Daniel's "words were heard from the first day" (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.12">Da 10:12</reference>), the good angel did not come to him until more than three weeks had elapsed (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.4">Da 10:4</reference>).<div eID="gen22083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22084" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one and twenty days--</hi>answering to the three weeks of Daniel's mourning (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.2">Da 10:2</reference>).<div eID="gen22084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22085" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Michael--</hi>that is, "Who is like God?" Though an archangel, "one of the chief princes," Michael was not to be compared to God.<div eID="gen22085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22086" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">help me--</hi>Michael, as patron of Israel before God (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.21">Da 10:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.12.1">12:1</reference>), "helped" to influence the Persian king to permit the Jews' return to Jerusalem.<div eID="gen22086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22087" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I remained--</hi>I was detained there with the kings of Persia, that is, with the angel of the Persian rulers, with whom I had to contend, and from whom I should not have got free, but for the help of Michael. Gesenius translates, "I obtained the ascendency," that is, I gained my point against the adverse angel of Persia, so as to influence the Persian authorities to favor Israel's restoration. <div eID="gen22087" type="x-p"/>
entries.1b83c46ffab8faf91e8c1fb7a43e18fbb0562bc7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12176"/><div sID="gen22088" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12176"/><hi type="bold">14. what shall befall thy people in the latter days--</hi>an intimation that the prophecy, besides describing the doings of Antiochus, reaches to the concluding calamities of Israel's history, prior to the nation's full restoration at Christ's coming--calamities of which Antiochus' persecutions were the type.<div eID="gen22088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22089" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vision is for many days--</hi>that is, extends far into the future. <div eID="gen22089" type="x-p"/>
entries.417e964034e8ce3b01f6f271379a6794e5850edd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12177"/><div sID="gen22090" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12177"/><hi type="bold">15. face toward the ground--</hi>in humble reverence (<reference osisRef="Gen.19.1">Ge 19:1</reference>).<div eID="gen22090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22091" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dumb--</hi>with overwhelming awe. <div eID="gen22091" type="x-p"/>
entries.4db37b34e1d3d6842661a8216768b8e31a8393d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12178"/><div sID="gen22092" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12178"/><hi type="bold">16. touched my lips--</hi>the same significant action wherewith the Son of man accompanied His healing of the dumb (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.33">Mr 7:33</reference>). He alone can give spiritual utterance (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.6">Is 6:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.6.19">Ep 6:19</reference>), enabling one to "open the mouth boldly." The same one who makes dumb (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.15">Da 10:15</reference>) opens the mouth.<div eID="gen22092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22093" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sorrows--</hi>literally, "writhings" as of a woman in travail. <div eID="gen22093" type="x-p"/>
entries.2030b3d2fd05e81b356a0a62a444ad4d0c7aebb7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12179"/><div sID="gen22094" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12179"/><hi type="bold">17. this ... this my lord--</hi>to avoid the tautology in English Version, join rather "this," with "servant," "How can this servant of my lord (that is, how can I who am so feeble) talk with this my lord (who is so majestic)?" Thus Daniel gives the reason why he is so overwhelmed with awe [Maurer]. <div eID="gen22094" type="x-p"/>
entries.b9c97c53de25cfbc91aca24ead2dede94569ee63: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12180"/><div sID="gen22095" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12180"/><hi type="bold">18. again ... touched me--</hi>It was gradually that Daniel recovered his strength. Hence there was need of the second touch, that he might hear the angel with composure. <div eID="gen22095" type="x-p"/>
entries.18458ac2d9cf8b76c597c3839bdfa11fd8bf6245: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12181"/><div sID="gen22096" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12181"/><hi type="bold">19. peace be unto thee--</hi>God is favorable to thee and to thy people Israel. See <reference osisRef="Judg.13.21">Jud 13:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.13.22">22</reference>, as to the fear of some evil resulting from a vision of angels. <div eID="gen22096" type="x-p"/>
entries.88e96f414e26602218ac73ce91887a113cdeebe6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12182"/><div sID="gen22097" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12182"/><hi type="bold">20. Knowest thou wherefore--</hi>The angel asks, after Daniel had recovered from his fright, whether he has understood what was revealed (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.13">Da 10:13</reference>). On Daniel, by his silence, intimating that he did understand, the angel declares he will return to renew the fight with the evil angel, the prince of Persia. This points to new difficulties to the Jews' restoration which would arise in the Persian court, but which would be counteracted by God, through the ministry of angels.<div eID="gen22097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22098" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prince of Grecia shall come--</hi>Alexander the Great, who conquered Persia, and favored the Jews [Calvin]. Rather, as the prince of Persia is an angel, representing the hostile world power, so the prince of Grecia is a fresh angelic adversary, representing Greece. When I am gone forth from conquering the Persian foe, a fresh one starts up, namely, the world power that succeeds Persia, Greece; Antiochus Epiphanes, and his antitype Antichrist, but him, too, with the help of Michael, Israel's champion, I shall overcome [Gejer]. <div eID="gen22098" type="x-p"/>
entries.57850f14113b50b7a6815ece1ef7fbc9eaa276fb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12183"/><div sID="gen22099" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12183"/><hi type="bold">21. noted in the scripture of truth--</hi>in the secret book of God's decrees (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.16">Psa 139:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.5.1">Re 5:1</reference>), which are truth, that is, the things which shall most surely come to pass, being determined by God (compare <reference osisRef="John.17.17">Joh 17:17</reference>).<div eID="gen22099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22100" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">none ... but Michael--</hi>To him alone of the angels the office of protecting Israel, in concert with the angelic speaker, was delegated; all the world powers were against Israel. <chapter eID="Dan.10"/>

entries.eb47334c950460e6535076038968cda0cf0c41d9: <div eID="gen33295" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen33296" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33297" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33297" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33296" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33298" type="x-p"/> This and the two following chapters give an account of Daniel's last vision, wherein the succession of the Persian and Grecian monarchies is described, together with the wars that should take place between Syria and Egypt under the latter monarchy. The last part of the vision (from <reference osisRef="Dan.11.36">Dan 11:36</reference>) seems to relate chiefly to the persecutions of the Church in the times of Antichrist, till it be purified from all its pollutions; after which will follow that glorious kingdom of the saints spoken of in the seventh and eighth chapters. This chapter begins with an account of Daniel's fasting and humiliation, <reference osisRef="Dan.10.1-Dan.10.3">Dan 10:1-3</reference>. Then we have a description of the Divine person who appeared to the prophet, not unlike him who appeared to the apostle in the isle of Patmos, vv. 4-21. See <reference osisRef="Rev.1.10-Rev.1.16">Rev 1:10-16</reference>. <div eID="gen33298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33299" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen33299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33300" type="x-p"/> In the third year of Cyrus - Which answers to the first year of Darius the Mede. <div eID="gen33300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33301" type="x-p"/> The time appointed was long - וצבא גדול vetsaba gadol, but the warfare long; there will be many contentions and wars before these things can be accomplished.
entries.33237ed47a632d17de14f2668ef2ffd37cf39f3a: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen33301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33302" type="x-p"/> I - was mourning three full weeks - The weeks are most probably dated from the time of the termination of the last vision. Calmet proves this by several reasons.
entries.c969bcc248fdae301b275d9e737c7550f28ef4b7: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen33302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33303" type="x-p"/> I ate no pleasant bread - This fast was rather a general abstinence; living all the while on coarse and unsavory food; drinking nothing but water; not using the bath, and most probably wearing haircloth next the skin, during the whole of the time.
entries.ef27626c02b649d5b258a23207c1796d4a2970e6: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen33303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33304" type="x-p"/> By the side of - Hiddekel - The same as the Tigris. the great river of Assyria; as the Euphrates of Syria, and the Nile of Egypt.
entries.804c163712c7164c6a15c7fe547b252ddcdff36e: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen33304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33305" type="x-p"/> Clothed in linen - The description is intended to point out the splendor of the garments. <div eID="gen33305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33306" type="x-p"/> Gold of Uphaz - The same as Ophir.
entries.04d6fa50c4f518797f49ce4e0979f54e7d4eb30a: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen33306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33307" type="x-p"/> His body also was like the beryl - The description of this person is very similar to that of our Lord in <reference osisRef="Rev.1.13-Rev.1.15">Rev 1:13-15</reference>.
entries.49853cbcd4466b7311005c7e841c12271d302699: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen33307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33308" type="x-p"/> The men that were with me saw not the vision - An exactly parallel case with what occurred at the conversion of Saul of Tarsus, <reference osisRef="Act.9.7">Act 9:7</reference>. There was a Divine influence which they all felt, but only Daniel saw the corporeal appearance.
entries.18815e04299033f4b678075a8d9ac97dfc641675: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen33308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33309" type="x-p"/> Was I in a deep sleep - I fell into a swoon.
entries.a3ffbbcd14d6fb228cccc7ebfbf930e24d56f33a: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen33309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33310" type="x-p"/> A hand touched me - Nothing was apparent or palpable but a hand. A hand had written Belshazzar's fate upon the wall; and the hand is frequently mentioned when the power or majesty of God is intended. Perhaps by hand God himself may be meant. It is remarkable that in a very ancient MS. of the Septuagint, more than a thousand years old, now in the imperial library of Vienna, adorned with paintings which have been engraved for the catalogue of Lambechius, and transferred to that of Nesselius, all the appearances of God are represented by a hand in the clouds.
entries.fb647dc1ff4992606e812960c56f6c60e960b3d8: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen33310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33311" type="x-p"/> I am come for thy words - On account of thy prayers I am sent to comfort and instruct thee.
entries.4c73d2d21cd67468cf8625f52cf7fead90e4a817: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen33311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33312" type="x-p"/> But the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me - I think it would go far to make a legend or a precarious tale of this important place to endeavor to maintain that either a good or evil Angel Is intended here. Cyrus alone was the prince of Persia, and God had destined him to be the deliverer of his people; but there were some matters, of which we are not informed, that caused him to hesitate for some time. Fearing, probably, the greatness of the work, and not being fully satisfied of his ability to execute it, he therefore for a time resisted the secret inspirations which God had sent him. The opposition might be in reference to the building of the temple. <div eID="gen33312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33313" type="x-p"/> But lo, Michael - Gabriel, who speaks, did not leave Cyrus till Michael came to take his place. Michael, he who is like God, sometimes appears to signify the Messiah, at other times the highest or chief archangel. Indeed there is no archangel mentioned in the whole Scripture but this one. See <reference osisRef="Jde.1.9">Jde 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.12.7">Rev 12:7</reference>.
entries.49ce0c25978ce67eb0ea375b7533da004d57393c: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen33313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33314" type="x-p"/> For yet the vision is for many days - There are many things which remain yet to be revealed, and the time of their accomplishment is very distant.
entries.333bc3d96766af01a4f8061576525c3ea1c9c580: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen33314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33315" type="x-p"/> I set my face toward the ground - He was standing upright, <reference osisRef="Dan.10.11">Dan 10:11</reference>, and he now bent his body in reverence, and looked down upon the ground. <div eID="gen33315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33316" type="x-p"/> And became dumb - Found himself unable to speak.
entries.551ba7ea7d0f6368a7619a05c47ed784ee418be3: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen33316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33317" type="x-p"/> Like the similitude of the sons of men - I think Gabriel is here meant, who appeared to Daniel in a human form; and so in <reference osisRef="Dan.10.18">Dan 10:18</reference>, and see also <reference osisRef="Dan.9.21">Dan 9:21</reference>. <div eID="gen33317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33318" type="x-p"/> Touched my lips - Before this he was unable to speak. <div eID="gen33318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33319" type="x-p"/> By the vision - The vision that I have already had, and of which I have not a proper knowledge has greatly afflicted me, because I see it intimates grievous calamities to my people. See <reference osisRef="Dan.9.26">Dan 9:26</reference>.
entries.15d7a1729585d3bb90235b0b3822b2fc9fbde8ea: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen33319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33320" type="x-p"/> Neither is there breath - He could not breathe freely; he was almost suffocated with sorrow.
entries.f81a09dd9c489442a9b004fc010e37e95ebe1bfd: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen33320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33321" type="x-p"/> O man, greatly beloved - איש חמדות ish chamudoth, man of delights; the most amiable of men. <div eID="gen33321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33322" type="x-p"/> Let my lord speak - I am now so strengthened and encouraged, that I shall be able to bear any revelation that thou mayest make.
entries.b362ff1e05f4d09a00e62044a54521857d5d938c: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen33322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33323" type="x-p"/> Knowest thou wherefore I come - So high art thou in the favor of God, that he hath sent me unto thee to give thee farther satisfaction; though I was elsewhere employed upon a most important mission, and I must speedily return to accomplish it, viz.: - <div eID="gen33323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33324" type="x-p"/> To fight with the king of Persia - To remove all the scruples of Cyrus, and to excite him to do all that God designs him to do for the restoration of my people, and the rebuilding of the city and temple of Jerusalem. Nothing less than a supernatural agency in the mind of Cyrus can account for his decree in favor of the Jews. He had no natural, no political inclination to it; and his reluctance to obey the heavenly motions is here represented as a fight between him and the angel. <div eID="gen33324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33325" type="x-p"/> The prince of Grecia shall come - I believe this refers to Alexander the Great, who was to destroy the Persian empire. See <reference osisRef="Dan.11.2-Dan.11.3">Dan 11:2-3</reference> (note).
entries.08399f1647ba5abf9eb0568cc5ae6f491fec680a: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen33325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33326" type="x-p"/> Noted in the scripture of truth - Perhaps this refers to what he had already written down. See the preceding visions, which Daniel did not fully understand, though a general impression from them had filled his heart with sorrow. <div eID="gen33326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33327" type="x-p"/> Michael your prince - The archangel mentioned before, <reference osisRef="Dan.10.13">Dan 10:13</reference>, and who has been always supposed to be appointed by God as the guardian of the Jewish nation. It appears that God chose to make use of the ministry of angels in this work; that angels, as they could be only in one place at one time, could not produce influence where they were not; and that, to carry on the operation on the mind of the Persian king, it was necessary that either Gabriel or Michael should be present with him, and when one went on another commission another took his place; see <reference osisRef="Dan.10.13">Dan 10:13</reference>. But we know so little of the invisible world that we cannot safely affirm any thing positively.  <chapter eID="Dan.10"/> <div eID="gen33327" type="x-p"/>

entries.8748d98e8af7ad15b2ff2255083eec1ae5da2e03: <div eID="gen15972" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Revelation Regarding the Affliction of the People of God on the Part of the Rulers of the World Till the Consummation of the Kingdom of God - <reference osisRef="Dan.10.12">Daniel 10-12</reference></title> <div sID="gen15973" type="x-p"/> In the third year of the reign of Cyrus, Daniel received the last revelation regarding the future of his people, which gives a fuller unfolding of the hostile attitude of the world-power toward the people and the kingdom of God from the time of the Persian dominion to the end of the days, as well as regarding the powerful protection which the covenant people shall experience amid the severe oppressions they would be exposed to for their purification. This revelation connects itself, both as to its contents and form, so closely with Daniel 8, that it is to be viewed as a further unfolding of that prophecy, and serves for the illustration and confirmation of that which was announced to the prophet shortly before the destruction of the Chaldean world-kingdom regarding the world-kingdoms that were to follow, and their relation to the theocracy. It consists of three parts: - (1.) There is the description of the appearance of God as to its nature, the impression it produced on the prophet, and its object (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.1-Dan.11.2">Daniel 10:1-11:2</reference> <hi type="italic">a</hi>). (2.) The unveiling of the future, in brief statements regarding the relation of the Persian and the Javanic world-kingdoms to Israel, and in more comprehensive descriptions of the wars of the kings of the north and the south for the supremacy, with the hostilities thence arising against the kingdom of God - hostilities which aim at its destruction, but which, because of the powerful succour which is rendered to Israel by Michael the angel-prince, shall come to an end in the destruction of the enemy of God and the final salvation of the people of God (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.2">Daniel 11:2</reference> <hi type="italic">b</hi>-12:3). (3.) This revelation concludes with the definition of the duration of the time of oppression, and with the command given to Daniel to seal up the words, together with the prophecy, till the time of the end, and to rest till the end come: “For thou shalt rest and stand in thy lot at the end of the days” (<reference osisRef="Dan.12.4-Dan.12.13">Dan 12:4-13</reference>). <div eID="gen15973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15974" type="x-p"/> If we attentively examine first of all the form of this revelation, namely, the manifestation of God, by which there is given to Daniel the understanding of the events of the future (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.14">Dan 10:14</reference>, cf. Daniel 11 and <reference osisRef="Dan.12.1-Dan.12.13">Dan 12:1-13</reference>), this revelation will be found to be distinguished from all the others in this, that it is communicated partly by supernatural illumination for the interpretation of the dream-vision, partly by visions, partly by the appearance of angels. Auberlen (<hi type="italic">d. Proph. Daniel</hi> p. 91f.) has already referred to this distinction, and therein has found a beautiful and noteworthy progression, namely, that the one revelation always prepares the way, in a material and formal respect, for that which follows, from which we may see how God gradually prepared the prophet for the reception of still more definite disclosures. “First Nebuchadnezzar dreams, and Daniel simply interprets (Daniel 2 and 4); afterwards Daniel himself has a dream, but as yet it is only as a vision in a dream of the night (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.1-Dan.7.2">Dan 7:1-2</reference>); then follows a vision in a waking state (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.1-Dan.8.3">Dan 8:1-3</reference>); and finally, in the last two revelations (Daniel 9 and 10-12), when Daniel, now a feeble, trembling (?) old man (Dan 10:8.), is already almost transplanted out of this world - now the ecstatic state seems to be no longer necessary for him. Now in his usual state he sees and hears angels speak like men, while his companions do not see the appearances from the higher world, and are only overwhelmed with terror, like those who accompanied Paul to Damascus (Dan 9:20., Dan 10:4., cf. Acts of Ap. <reference osisRef="Acts.9.7">Act 9:7</reference>).” It is true, indeed, that, as Aub. remarks, there is a progression from interpreting of dreams to the receiving of visions in dreams and in the waking state, but by this reference neither are the actual contents of the revelation given in different forms perfectly comprehended, nor still less is the meaning of the difference made clear. Auberlen, in thus representing the distinction, has left out of view the circumstance, that the visions in Daniel 7 and 8 are also interpreted to Daniel by an angel; moreover, that the revelation in Daniel 8 does not merely consist of a vision, in which Daniel sees the destruction of the Persian world-kingdom by the Javanic under the figure of a he-goat casting down the ram, but that Daniel, after this vision, also hears an angel speak, and a voice comes to him from above the waters of the Ulai which commands the angel Gabriel to explain the vision to the seer (Dan 8:13.), and that this second part of that revelation has a great likeness to that in <reference osisRef="Dan.10.12">Daniel 10-12</reference>; finally, that the same angel Gabriel again appears in Daniel 9, and brings to Daniel the revelation regarding the seventy weeks (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.24-Dan.9.27">Dan 9:24-27</reference>). But as to the interpretation of these revelations given in different forms, this difference is conditioned partly by the subjective relations sustained by the recipients to God, while, on the other hand, the form is in the most intimate manner connected with the contents of the revelation, and indeed in a way wholly different and much deeper than Auberlen thinks, if he therein sees only the material progression to greater speciality in the prophecy. <div eID="gen15974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15975" type="x-p"/> To comprehend the meaning of the divine revelation in <reference osisRef="Dan.10.12">Daniel 10-12</reference>, we must examine more closely the resemblance which it presents to <reference osisRef="Dan.8.13">Dan 8:13</reference>-19. As in the vision Daniel 8, which points to the oppression of the time of the end (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.17">Dan 8:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.19">Dan 8:19</reference>), Daniel heard a voice from the Ulai (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.16">Dan 8:16</reference>), so in Daniel 10 and <reference osisRef="Dan.12.1-Dan.12.13">Dan 12:1-13</reference> the personage from whom that voice proceeded appears within the circle of Daniel’s vision, and announces to him what shall happen to his people הימים בּאחרית (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.14">Dan 10:14</reference>). This celestial person appears to him in such awful divine majesty, that he falls to the ground on hearing his voice, as already in Dan 8:17. on hearing his voice and message, so that he feared he should perish; and it was only by repeated supernatural consolation and strengthening that he was able to stand erect again, and was made capable of hearing the revelation. The heavenly being who appears to him resembles in appearance the glory of Jehovah which Ezekiel had seen by the river Chaboras (Chebar); and this appearance of the man clothed in linen prepared the contents of his revelation, for God so manifested Himself to Daniel (as He will approve Himself to His people in the times of the future great tribulation) as He who in judgment and in righteousness rules the affairs of the world-kingdoms and of the kingdom of God, and conducts them to the issues foreseen; so that the effect of His appearance on Daniel formed a pre-intimation and a pledge of that which would happen to the people of Daniel in the future. As Daniel was thrown to the ground by the divine majesty of the man clothed in linen, but was raised up again by a supernatural hand, so shall the people of God be thrown to the ground by the fearful judgments that shall pass over them, but shall again be raised up by the all-powerful help of their God and His angel-prince Michael, and shall be strengthened to endure the tribulation. According to this, the very appearance of God has prophetic significance; and the reason why this last vision is communicated to Daniel neither by a vision nor by angels, but by a majestic Theophany, does not lie in the more definite disclosures which should be given to him regarding the future, but only in this, that the revelation, as is mentioned in the superscription, <reference osisRef="Dan.10.1">Dan 10:1</reference>, places in view the גּדול וצבא אמת (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.1">Dan 10:1</reference>). <div eID="gen15975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15976" type="x-p"/> Of this oppression, that spoken of in Daniel 8, which should come upon the people of God from the fierce and cunning king seen as a little horn, forms a type; therefore Daniel hears the voice from the waters of the Ulai. That which is there briefly indicated, is in <reference osisRef="Dan.10.12">Daniel 10-12</reference> further extended and completed. In regard to the definiteness of the prediction, the revelation in <reference osisRef="Dan.10.12">Daniel 10-12</reference> does not go beyond that in Daniel 8; but it does so with respect to the detailed description found in it of the wars of the world-rulers against one another and against the people of God, as well as in this, that it opens a glimpse into the spirit-world, and gives disclosures regarding the unseen spiritual powers who mingle in the history of nations. But over these powers God the Lord exercises dominion, and helps His people to obtain a victory over all their enemies. To reveal this, and in actual fact to attest it to the prophet, and through him to the church of God of all times, is the object of the Theophany, which is circumstantially described in Daniel 10 for the sake of its prophetical character. <div eID="gen15976" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Theophany - <reference osisRef="Dan.10.11">Daniel 10-11</reference>:2a</title> <title type="x-s2">The Introduction to the Following Manifestation of God - <reference osisRef="Dan.10.1-Dan.10.3">Dan 10:1-3</reference></title> <div sID="gen15977" type="x-p"/> This verse is to be regarded as an inscription or general statement of the substance of it.
